needs: Chapter 128 — Neurologic Diseases and Opportunistic Infections in HIV
questions.stem: A 35-year-old man was brought in by ambulance after being found unconscious. His partner gave a collateral history of preceding symptoms for 3 weeks of fevers, headaches, and new-onset seizures. He was known to have HIV but had not been on antiretroviral therapy or taking antibiotic prophylaxis. The patient was originally from Brazil but immigrated to the United States 2 years ago. On physical exam, the patient was somnolent with rightsided upper and lower extremity weakness. Investigations: CD4 count 23 cells/μL HIV viral load 76,850 copies/mL Serum Toxoplasma IgG serologies negative CSF EBV PCR negative CSF VDRL negative MRI brain: 3 discrete hypodense masses in the cerebral cortex with contrast ring enhancement
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chagas brain abscess In patients from endemic regions, Trypanosoma cruzi can cause acute or reactivation disease, particularly in patients with advanced AIDS. The most common presentation is CNS reactivation leading to meningoencephalitis or brain abscesses, which presents very similarly to Toxoplasma with ring-enhancing lesions on MRI imaging. The negative serum Toxoplasma serologies and EBV PCR in the CSF make other causes such as toxoplasmic encephalitis or primary CNS lymphoma less likely while the patient’s country of origin in South America is endemic for Chagas disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 6 Q24

needs: Chapter 310 — Infections in the Immunocompromised Host
questions.stem: A 67-year-old man presented with a 2-week history of headache, nausea, vomiting, neck pain, and low-grade fever. He underwent orthotopic liver transplantation for alcoholic cirrhosis 6 months prior and was on high-dose steroids for induction and tacrolimus and mycophenolate for maintenance immunosuppression. He was on secondary prophylaxis with valganciclovir for CMV syndrome. MRI brain: multiple rim-enhancing lesions along the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles, corpus callosum, and cerebellum.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?
questions.explanation: Perform a brain biopsy The differential for this presentation is too broad, and empiricism may lead to bad outcomes. The patient underwent a stereotactic needle biopsy of the right frontal lesion. Pathology showed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma that was CD20-positive. In situ hybridization was positive for EBVencoded small RNA (EBER). A PET scan showed no activity outside of the CNS. This was a case of posttransplant primary CNS lymphoma, which carries a dismal prognosis.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q24

questions.question: A pregnant woman presents at 12 weeks gestational age with a Toxoplasma serology positive for IgM.
questions.question_raw: A pregnant female presents at 12 weeks GA with a toxoplasma serology positive for IgM.

parts.text: What 2 non-serological tests would you perform?
What 1 treatment would you start?
If she is now at 24 weeks, what would the treatment of choice be?

parts_raw.text: What 2 non-serological tests would you perform?
What 1 treatment would you start?
If it is now at 24 weeks, what would the treatment of choice be?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Amniotic fluid PCR for T. gondii DNA, performed at 18 weeks of gestation or later. (2) Fetal ultrasound looking for abnormalities suggestive of congenital toxoplasmosis (hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications). b) Spiramycin, because the infection was acquired before 14 weeks of gestation (reduces transplacental transmission; pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine is not offered before 14 weeks owing to teratogenicity). c) At 24 weeks (>=14 weeks): pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine plus folinic acid; switch to/continue this if amniotic fluid PCR is positive or ultrasound is abnormal.

cohort_answer.text: Non-serological tests: Amnio PCR at 18 weeks onwards; Fetal u/s. || Treatment: Spiramycin (maximum efficacy if given within 8 weeks of seroconversion). || At 24 weeks: Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin.

questions.question: IgG avidity testing in a pregnant woman with a positive Toxoplasma IgM.

parts.text: Briefly describe IgG avidity testing in the context of a pregnant woman with a positive Toxoplasma IgM.
What are the implications to the fetus if it is highly avid IgG?

parts_raw.text: Briefly describe the IgG avidity testing in the context of a pregnant female with a positive toxoplasma IgM.
What are the implications to the fetus if it is highly avid IgG?

questions.model_answer: a) During acute infection IgG antibodies bind antigen weakly (low avidity), whereas chronic infection produces strongly binding (high-avidity) antibodies; protein-denaturing reagents (e.g., urea) dissociate weakly bound complexes. It is used only as a confirmatory test alongside a battery of tests, and is most useful in the first 16 weeks of gestation: a high-avidity result then indicates infection acquired at least 3-5 months earlier (>=4 months by VIDAS). A low/equivocal result cannot be used to date infection because it may persist for months to years. b) A highly avid IgG result in the first 16 weeks means the infection was acquired at least 3-5 months earlier, i.e., before conception; the fetus is essentially not at risk for congenital toxoplasmosis, and further testing/treatment (amniotic fluid PCR, spiramycin) may be avoided.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman with HIV presents with seizures, weakness, and confusion. Imaging shows an intracranial gray matter lesion with mass effect and no herniation. No CSF parameters are given. You suspect toxoplasmosis.
questions.question_raw: 34yo woman with HIV, seizures, weakness, confusion. Intracranial lesion in gray matter with mass effect, no herniation. No CSF parameters given/ appears to be done. You suspect toxo.

parts.text: What is your treatment regimen?
This woman is now 16 weeks pregnant - how would you treat?
What is the most likely alternative diagnosis?

parts_raw.text: What is your treatment regimen
THIS woman is now 16 wks pregnant – how to treat?
What is the most likely alternative dx?

questions.model_answer: a) Pyrimethamine 200 mg PO loading dose, then 50 mg/day (<60 kg) to 75 mg/day (>=60 kg), PLUS sulfadiazine 1000 mg (<60 kg) to 1500 mg (>=60 kg) q6h, PLUS folinic acid (leucovorin) 10-20 mg/day (up to 50 mg/day); acute therapy for at least 3-6 weeks, followed by maintenance (secondary prophylaxis). b) At 16 weeks (>=14 weeks) pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine-folinic acid is acceptable, so the same regimen can be used (pyrimethamine is avoided only in the first trimester); pyrimethamine-clindamycin-folinic acid is an alternative. c) Primary CNS lymphoma.

questions.question: A woman with HIV (CD4 72) presents with seizure and focal neurologic deficits. CT head shows 3 large gray matter lesions, the largest about 3 cm. She has never travelled and was born in Canada.
questions.question_raw: A woman who has HIV (CD4 72) presents with seizure/focal neurologic deficits. CT head demonstrates 3 large grey matter lesions, largest ~3 cm. She has not travelled anywhere and she was born in Canada – (2019)

parts.text: You suspect these lesions are due to toxoplasmosis - what is the first-line therapy for this condition?
How would you treat this patient if she were 16 weeks pregnant?
What would your top differential diagnosis be if this ended up not being toxoplasmosis?

parts_raw.text: A) You suspect these lesions are due to toxoplasmosis - what is the first line therapy for this condition?
B) How would you treat this patient if she were 16 weeks pregnant?
C) What would your top differential diagnosis be if this ended up not being toxoplasmosis?

questions.model_answer: a) Pyrimethamine 200 mg PO load, then 50-75 mg/day, PLUS sulfadiazine 1000-1500 mg q6h, PLUS folinic acid 10-20 mg/day (up to 50 mg/day) for at least 3-6 weeks, followed by maintenance therapy until CD4 >200 for at least 6 months on ART. b) At 16 weeks (>=14 weeks) pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine-folinic acid can be used (pyrimethamine avoided only in the first trimester); same regimen, with alternative pyrimethamine-clindamycin-folinic acid. c) Primary CNS lymphoma.

cohort_answer.text: First line therapy: Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin for 6 weeks, followed by TMP/SMX 1 DS BID until VL suppressed and CD4 >200 for 3 months (if unable to use sulfadiazine need alternative PJP proph agent). If pregnant: HIV+ with brain lesions + pregnant = wait until 2nd trimester to use pyrimethamine, otherwise treat as per adult; discuss risks/benefits of secondary prophylaxis with TMPSMX during pregnancy; spiramycin recommended to prevent congenital transmission during primary infection in pregnancy but does not treat fetal infection; pyrimethamine/sulfadiazine/leucovorin recommended for pregnant women with strong suspicion of fetal infection, pyrimethamine avoided in first trimester due to teratogenicity. Top differential: Primary CNS lymphoma (median age 35 in HIV, often multiple lesions); other ddx: TB, PML (white matter lesions), Cryptococcal meningitis (not typical imaging), Neurocysticercosis (no travel), Bartonellosis (no exposures)

questions.question: A 1-month-old infant was seen by ophthalmology and had findings suggestive of toxoplasmosis on eye exam.
questions.question_raw: 1 month old went to the ophthalmologist and had findings suggestive toxoplasmosis on eye exam.

parts.text: What are the three common findings in a symptomatic neonate with congenital toxoplasmosis?
Name 3 serologic test results that would be diagnostic for congenital toxoplasmosis.
Name 3 drugs that are the first-line treatment of congenital toxoplasmosis.

parts_raw.text: What are the three common findings in a neonate with congenital toxo that is symptomatic
Name 3 serologic tests results that would be diagnostic for congenital toxoplasmosis
Name 3 drugs that are the first line treatment of congenital toxoplasmosis

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Chorioretinitis. (2) Hydrocephalus. (3) Intracranial (brain) calcifications - the classic triad of major clinical signs. b) (1) Positive T. gondii IgM (in serum obtained after 5 days of life, to exclude maternal contamination). (2) Positive IgA (after 10 days of life). (3) Positive IgE (or IgM-ISAGA); demonstration of intrathecal/locally produced specific antibody is also diagnostic. c) (1) Pyrimethamine. (2) Sulfadiazine. (3) Folinic acid (leucovorin).

questions.question: A patient has toxoplasmosis but cannot receive sulfadiazine.
questions.question_raw: Q50 (2015). Patient has toxoplasmosis, no sulfadiazine.

parts.text: What are 2 other treatment options?
The patient has Pneumocystis pneumonia but cannot receive co-trimoxazole (septra). What are 2 other options for treatment?

parts_raw.text: A) What are 2 other treatment options?
B) Patient has PCP, no septra. What are 2 other options for treatment?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Pyrimethamine plus clindamycin (with folinic acid). (2) Pyrimethamine (or sulfadiazine) plus atovaquone; TMP-SMX (10 mg/kg/day of the trimethoprim component) is a further alternative. Note: if a pyrimethamine-clindamycin regimen is used, add separate PCP prophylaxis. b) For Pneumocystis pneumonia without co-trimoxazole: (1) Clindamycin plus primaquine. (2) IV pentamidine (severe disease); atovaquone or dapsone-trimethoprim are options for mild-moderate disease.
questions.beyond_mandell: Part b (Pneumocystis pneumonia therapy) is not covered by this Toxoplasma chapter; regimens are per IDSA/NIH Guidelines for the Prevention and Treatment of Opportunistic Infections in Adults with HIV.

cohort_answer.text: A) Alternative: Pyrimethamine + Clindamycin; Pyrimethamine + Atovaquone. B) Mild: Clindamycin + primaquine, Dapsone + trimethoprim, Atovaquone. Moderate: Clindamycin + primaquine, Dapsone + trimethoprim. Severe: Clindamycin + primaquine, IV pentamidine.

questions.question: A man with vasculitis on steroids has ring-enhancing lesions in the brain and lung nodules. List three possible organisms and the first-line empiric treatment regimen.

parts.text: List three possible organisms and the first-line empiric treatment regimen for an immunosuppressed patient with ring-enhancing brain lesions and lung nodules.

parts_raw.text: Guy with vasculitis on steroids who has ring enhancing lesions in brain and lung nodules. List 3 possible organisms and first line empiric treatment regimen

questions.model_answer: Three organisms: (1) Nocardia species; (2) Staphylococcus aureus; (3) Streptococcus anginosus group (also consider Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Cryptococcus, Toxoplasma, Aspergillus). Empiric regimen: cover pyogenic brain abscess (e.g., ceftriaxone + vancomycin + metronidazole) PLUS anti-Nocardia therapy given the immunosuppression and combined brain/lung picture — TMP-SMX plus imipenem or meropenem, plus amikacin (or ceftriaxone/linezolid), then de-escalate after speciation and susceptibilities.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the Nocardia arm is grounded in this chapter; the broader brain-abscess differential and empiric bacterial/TB/fungal coverage rest on standard CNS-infection references (Mandell brain abscess chapter/IDSA).

cohort_answer.text: Possible organisms: Nocardia, Staph aureus, Streptococcus anginosus. Empiric treatment: Ceftriaxone, vanco, metro (empiric bacterial coverage); Septra, imipenem +/- amikacin (Nocardia); TB - RIPE + steroids if meningitis; Cryptococcus - amphoB + flucytosine, then fluconazole

questions.question: A person has a fluctuant mass in his neck with erythema, swelling and tenderness. For each scenario, name the most common pathogen and the most appropriate specimen and microbiologic test.
questions.question_raw: Person has a fluctuant mass in his neck with erythema, swelling and tenderness. For the following scenarios, name the most common pathogen and the most appropriate specimen and microbiologic test.

parts.text: Recently ate steak tartare.
Immigrant from Vietnam, also has cough and weight loss over a few weeks.
Bitten by a rabbit on the shoulder.
Inflamed tonsils with exudate.

parts_raw.text: Recently ate steak tartar
Immigrant from Vietnam, also has cough and weight loss over few weeks
Bit by a rabbit on the shoulder
Inflamed tonsils with exudate

questions.model_answer:
a) Toxoplasma gondii; specimen: serum; test: Toxoplasma IgG/IgM serology (acute and convalescent). [Beyond this chapter.]
b) Mycobacterium tuberculosis (cervical scrofula); specimen: fine-needle aspirate or excisional lymph node biopsy; test: AFB smear, mycobacterial culture and NAAT. [Beyond this chapter.]
c) Francisella tularensis (ulceroglandular tularemia); specimen: serum (organism rarely seen/grown, and culture is hazardous); test: tube- or micro-agglutination serology, acute and convalescent (fourfold rise); node aspirate can be sent for PCR/culture on cysteine-enriched media at a reference lab under BSL-3.
d) Streptococcus pyogenes; specimen: throat swab; test: rapid antigen and/or throat culture. [Beyond this chapter.]
questions.beyond_mandell: Parts a, b and d (Toxoplasma, TB adenitis, S. pyogenes) are outside the Francisella chapter; answered from standard ID knowledge (Mandell relevant chapters/IDSA).

cohort_answer.text: Steak tartar: Toxoplasma gondii. Blood serology acute and convalescent. Immigrant from Vietnam: Tuberculosis adenitis - fine needle aspiration or excisional biopsy for AFB and mycobacterial culture. Rabbit bite: Francisella tularensis, blood serology at time of presentation and 2-4 weeks after. Inflamed tonsils: Strep pyogenes. Pharyngeal culture. Parapharyngeal/retropharyngeal collection may need to be drained and can be cultured

questions.question: For each of the following Toxoplasma serology results, give the interpretation, what you would do, and further suggestions.
questions.question_raw: Toxo scenarios. Give interpretation, what do you do, and further suggestions.

parts.text: IgG negative / IgM negative?
IgG positive / IgM negative?
IgG positive / IgM positive?

parts_raw.text: IgG NEG/IgM NEG?
IgG POS/IgM NEG?
IgG POS/IgM POS?

questions.model_answer: a) No serologic evidence of Toxoplasma infection (susceptible). Do nothing diagnostically; if pregnant, counsel on primary prevention and consider follow-up testing to detect seroconversion. b) Chronic/past infection acquired in the distant past with immunity; in the first two trimesters this indicates essentially no risk to the fetus (exception: severely immunodeficient patients). No further action needed. c) Possible acute infection but timing cannot be established from a single sample. Send serum to a reference laboratory for a confirmatory battery, including IgG avidity; if pregnant, offer amniotic fluid PCR (at >=18 weeks) and fetal ultrasound, and consider treatment (spiramycin if <14 weeks, pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine-folinic acid if >=14 weeks).

cohort_answer.text: IgG NEG/IgM NEG: no infection, do nothing. IgG POS/IgM NEG: remote infection with immunity. IgG POS/IgM POS: possibly acute infection but can't tell how acute, consider IgG avidity testing; look for signs of CNS infection, eye disease, or pregnancy - if present consider treatment with pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine. (In acute infection, IgM usually appears within 1 week and rises, then declines/disappears variably (sometimes over months); IgG follows within ~2 weeks, peaks ~8 weeks, generally persists for life; no direct correlation between IgG titer height and proximity of infection.)

questions.question: A man with HIV and CD4 <50 had stopped co-trimoxazole (septra) because of Stevens-Johnson syndrome. He presents with 2 weeks of fever and neurologic symptoms. CT shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions without mass effect.
questions.question_raw: HIV man with CD4 <50. Had stopped Septra because of SJS. 2 weeks of fever and neurologic symptoms. CT shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions without mass effect.

parts.text: What would you treat with and for how long? What secondary prophylaxis? When do you stop?

parts_raw.text: What to treat with and for how long? What secondary ppx? When do you stop?

questions.model_answer: Because of the sulfa allergy (SJS), avoid sulfadiazine and TMP-SMX. Treat with pyrimethamine (200 mg load, then 50-75 mg/day) PLUS clindamycin (600 mg q6h, up to 1200 mg q6h) PLUS folinic acid 10-20 mg/day. Acute therapy for at least 3 weeks and usually 6 weeks (longer if incomplete response). Follow with secondary prophylaxis (maintenance) using the same agents at reduced dose (pyrimethamine 25-50 mg/day plus clindamycin 600 mg q8h plus folinic acid). Because clindamycin-pyrimethamine has no anti-Pneumocystis activity, add PCP prophylaxis (e.g., atovaquone or aerosolized pentamidine). Stop maintenance therapy when CD4 rises above 200 cells/mm3 and is sustained for at least 6 months on ART with resolution of disease.

cohort_answer.text: Toxoplasmosis gondii. HIV+ CD4<100 with space-occupying lesion involving gray matter: ddx is either toxo or lymphoma. If in endemic area: fungal, mycobacterial and parasitic also possible

questions.question: For the Toxoplasma serology results IgG-/IgM-, IgG+/IgM-, and IgG+/IgM+, give the interpretation, what you would do, and further investigations.
questions.question_raw: Toxoplasmosis scenario. Give interpretation, what do you do, and further investigations for: IgG-/IgM-; IgG+/IgM-; IgG+/IgM+

parts.text: Give the interpretation, what you would do, and further investigations for IgG-/IgM-, IgG+/IgM-, and IgG+/IgM+.

parts_raw.text: Give interpretation, what do you do, and further investigations

questions.model_answer: IgG-/IgM-: No evidence of Toxoplasma infection (susceptible); no acute or past infection. If pregnant, counsel on primary prevention and consider follow-up serology to detect seroconversion. IgG+/IgM-: Chronic/past infection, acquired in the distant past (before gestation); essentially no fetal risk in the first two trimesters (exception: severe immunodeficiency); no further testing needed. IgG+/IgM+: Possible acute infection but timing indeterminate; send to a reference laboratory for a confirmatory battery including IgG avidity to confirm/exclude recent infection. If pregnant with confirmed/likely recent infection, offer amniotic fluid PCR (at >=18 weeks) and fetal ultrasound.

cohort_answer.text: IgG-/IgM-: no evidence of toxo. IgG+/IgM-: probably past infection >6 months prior to pregnancy, no further testing. IgG+/IgM+: if seroconversion, may offer amniocentesis PCR and fetal US. Can send for Toxo IgG avidity testing to confirm it's a recent infection.

questions.question: A woman who is 6 weeks pregnant reports a possible exposure to Toxoplasma. Serology reveals positive IgG and positive IgM.
questions.question_raw: Evaluation of pregnant female with ?toxo. Scenario with woman who is 6 weeks pregnant, possible exposure to toxo. Serology reveals + IgG and IgM.

parts.text: What is one test you can do to determine timing of infection?
Explain briefly how you would interpret the results of this test and why.

parts_raw.text: What is one test you can do to determine timing of infection?
Explain briefly how you would interpret the results of this test and why?

questions.model_answer: a) IgG avidity test (the differential agglutination [AC/HS] test is an acceptable alternative), performed as a confirmatory test at a reference laboratory. b) Avidity reflects the strength of antibody-antigen binding: it is low early in acute infection and matures to high avidity with time. A HIGH-avidity result means the infection was acquired at least 3-5 months earlier (VIDAS assay: at least 4 months); in a woman within the first 16 weeks of gestation a high-avidity result therefore indicates the infection predates conception and the fetus is essentially not at risk, regardless of the positive IgM. A LOW or EQUIVOCAL result cannot be used to date the infection, because low/equivocal avidity can persist for months to years after primary infection; it must not be used alone and mandates a full battery of confirmatory tests.

cohort_answer.text: A) IgG avidity testing or AC/HS pattern. The differential agglutination test ("AC/HS test") uses two antigen preparations expressing determinants found early (AC antigen) or late (HS) in infection; ratios interpreted as acute, equivocal, non-acute or non-reactive; acute pattern may persist for a year+. Best used with a panel of other tests (e.g. TSP). The IgG avidity test measures antibody binding force, low early after infection, increasing with time; high avidity indicates infection occurred at least four months earlier. B) High-avidity IgG antibodies develop at least 12-16 weeks after infection, indicating infection acquired >16 weeks earlier. In a pregnant woman early in gestation, a high-avidity IgG result indicates the fetus is essentially not at risk for congenital toxo, regardless of IgM. For pregnant women >16 weeks GA, a high-avidity test at least shows infection acquired 12-16 weeks earlier (in this scenario, the NPV of amniotic fluid PCR would be higher). Low-avidity or equivocal results can persist for a year or more and must not be used alone to determine recent infection.

questions.question: A table of Toxoplasma serology results is provided.
questions.question_raw: Table of toxo serology.

parts.text: Which one needs confirmatory testing?
If congenital infection at 20 weeks gestation, what do you treat her with and for how long?
What 2 other investigations are required?

parts_raw.text: Which one needs confirmatory testing?
If congenital infection at 20 weeks gestation, what do you treat her with and for how long?
What 2 other investigations are required?

questions.model_answer: a) The positive IgM result. Only positive (or equivocal) IgM tests need to be sent for confirmatory testing at a reference laboratory, because a positive IgM may represent a false positive or persistence from chronic infection rather than recently acquired infection. b) Because infection/fetal involvement is confirmed at 20 weeks (i.e. at or after 14 weeks gestation), treat with pyrimethamine PLUS sulfadiazine PLUS folinic acid (leucovorin); if she had still been on spiramycin, switch to this combination once amniotic fluid PCR is positive or ultrasound is abnormal. Continue until delivery. c) (1) Amniotic fluid PCR for T. gondii, performed at 18 weeks of gestation or later. (2) Fetal ultrasound to detect abnormalities suggestive of congenital toxoplasmosis (e.g. hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications).

cohort_answer.text: A) A positive IgM test result requires further assessment with confirmatory testing at a reference laboratory. Confirm moms with positive screening (IgM+ or equivocal) during pregnancy; screen women suspected to have acute toxoplasmosis, with risk factors, symptoms, or immunocompromised (up to 50% of women have no risk factors or are asymptomatic). B) Spiramycin is indicated for patients confirmed/suspected infected before 14 weeks gestation, continued until delivery even if amniotic fluid PCR negative/US normal. Because spiramycin does not reliably cross the placenta, if fetal infection documented/highly suspected or maternal infection acquired at 14 weeks or later, recommend sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine, and folinic acid (10-20mg daily, during and 1 week after pyrimethamine). Pyrimethamine avoided in first 14 weeks (teratogenicity); consider clindamycin instead of pyrimethamine in early pregnancy with sulfadiazine before switching to pyrimethamine. Pyrimethamine + Sulfadiazine (+leucovorin), duration until delivery for mother, for baby until age 1. C) Fetal US (look for hydrocephalus, brain or hepatic calcifications, splenomegaly, ascites); PCR of amniotic fluid at 18 weeks (sensitivity 64%, specificity 100%, NPV 88%, PPV 100%). Amniotic fluid PCR considered for women with (1) diagnostic/highly suggestive serology, (2) fetal damage on US, or (3) significant immunosuppression (except AIDS).

questions.question: A pregnant woman was exposed at 19 weeks gestation to Toxoplasma and is now IgM positive.
questions.question_raw: Pregnant woman exposed at 19 weeks to toxoplasma. Now IgM +

parts.text: What investigations would you order and how would you manage this situation?

parts_raw.text: What investigations would you order and how would you manage this situation?

questions.model_answer: Investigations: (1) Send serum to a reference laboratory for confirmatory serology (battery of tests plus IgG avidity) to establish whether infection was acquired during gestation; if prior serology was negative, repeat testing in parallel to document IgG/IgM seroconversion. (2) If acute maternal infection is confirmed or highly suspected, perform amniotic fluid PCR for T. gondii at 18 weeks or later. (3) Fetal ultrasound to detect abnormalities (hydrocephalus, calcifications). Management: Because infection was acquired at/after 14 weeks (19 weeks here), institute pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine plus folinic acid rather than spiramycin, and continue treatment until delivery; switch definitively to this combination if amniotic fluid PCR is positive or ultrasound is abnormal. Consult a reference laboratory/expert.

cohort_answer.text: If previous serology negative, repeat serology to confirm IgG conversion and proceed with amniotic fluid PCR and fetal US. Otherwise send for confirmatory serological toxo profile with IgG avidity testing.

questions.question: Interpret the following Toxoplasma serology scenarios in a pregnant woman.
questions.question_raw: Q80 (2011 AM). Toxoplasma scenarios

parts.text: IgG negative / IgM negative?
IgG positive / IgM negative?
IgG positive / IgM positive?
IgG negative / IgM positive?

parts_raw.text: A. IgG NEG/IgM NEG?
B. IgG POS/IgM NEG?
C. IgG POS/IgM POS?
D. IgG NEG/IgM POS?

questions.model_answer: a) No serologic evidence of Toxoplasma infection (not toxoplasmosis). She is susceptible and at risk only if she acquires infection during pregnancy; provide primary-prevention counselling and follow-up testing. b) Chronic/past infection acquired before gestation. In the first two trimesters this almost always indicates chronic maternal infection with essentially no risk to the fetus (exception: severe immunodeficiency). c) Possible acute infection, but a positive IgM cannot date the infection (IgM may persist for months to years or be falsely positive); requires confirmatory reference-laboratory testing/IgG avidity to determine how recent the infection is. d) Most likely very early acute infection (IgG may not yet be detectable in the first ~2 weeks) or a false-positive IgM; requires confirmatory/repeat serology to distinguish acute infection from a false positive.

cohort_answer.text: A. Not toxo. B. Less likely acute toxo. C. Toxo but cannot really tell how acute infection is. D. Most likely acute toxo.

questions.question: Name two second-line treatments for each of the following infections.
questions.question_raw: Name two second-line treatments for the following infections

parts.text: PJP pneumonia (other than trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole).
Toxoplasmosis (other than pyrimethamine).
Stenotrophomonas (other than trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole).

parts_raw.text: PJP pneumonia (other than TMP-SMX)
Toxoplasmosis (other than pyrimethamine)
Stenotrophomonas (other than TMP-SMX)

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Clindamycin plus primaquine (preferred alternative, including for moderate-to-severe disease; check G6PD). (2) Atovaquone or oral TMP plus dapsone for mild-to-moderate disease; IV pentamidine for severe disease. b) (1) TMP-SMX. (2) Atovaquone (alone or with sulfadiazine); clindamycin can substitute for sulfadiazine in a pyrimethamine-based regimen. c) (1) A fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin or moxifloxacin). (2) Minocycline/tigecycline, or ceftazidime/cefiderocol.
questions.beyond_mandell: Toxoplasmosis and Stenotrophomonas regimens are not covered in this Pneumocystis chapter; those options rest on IDSA/CDC OI guidance and standard antimicrobial references.

cohort_answer.text:
PJP pneumonia: Mild to moderate: Atovaquone; Clindamycin-Primaquine; Dapsone/TMP. Severe disease: Clindamycin-Primaquine (check for G6PD); IV Pentamidine (toxic). Prophylaxis: Dapsone; Atovoquone; Aerosolized pentamidine
Toxoplasmosis: Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole monotherapy; Atovoquone alone; Atovoquone + sulfadiazine
Stenotrophomonas: Levofloxacin, moxi; Minocycline; Tigecycline; Ceftazidime (resistance is high); Colistin. Mechanism of resistance: multidrug-resistant efflux pumps, β-lactamases, and aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes, reduced permeability of the outer membrane

questions.question: There is a drug shortage in a hospital. How would you treat the following conditions if the usual first-line drug were not available? Give the drug you cannot use and treatment options for PJP, Toxoplasma, and Stenotrophomonas.
questions.question_raw: 18. Drug shortage in a hospital

parts.text: For PJP, Toxoplasma, and Stenotrophomonas, state the drug that cannot be used and give treatment options.

parts_raw.text: How would you treat the following conditions if the listed drug were not available? (3) Infection / Cannot Use / Treatment Options for: PJP, Toxoplasma, Stenotrophomonas

questions.model_answer: a) (1) PJP - cannot use TMP-SMX: use clindamycin plus primaquine (preferred alternative, check G6PD), or atovaquone / TMP plus dapsone for mild-to-moderate, or IV pentamidine for severe. (2) Toxoplasma - cannot use pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine: use TMP-SMX, or pyrimethamine plus clindamycin, or atovaquone-based regimens. (3) Stenotrophomonas - cannot use TMP-SMX: use levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, minocycline/tigecycline, or cefiderocol/ceftazidime.
questions.beyond_mandell: Toxoplasma and Stenotrophomonas alternatives are outside this chapter and rest on IDSA/CDC OI guidance and standard antimicrobial references.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man with HIV, CD4 count 50 cells/uL, non-adherent to antiretroviral therapy, presents with ataxia and vague neurologic symptoms and no headache. No focal deficits on examination. No travel history; lives in Toronto. No lumbar puncture performed. MRI brain shows diffuse multifocal lesions.
questions.question_raw: 50yo M HIV positive patient with CD4 count 50copies/mL, non-compliant with ART presenting with ataxia and vague neuro symptoms, no headaches. No focal neuro symptoms on exam. No history of travel, lives in Toronto. No LP given. MRI brain shows diffuse multifocal lesions.

parts.text: Give four pathogens and their associated syndromes to explain the clinical presentation.

parts_raw.text: Give 4 pathogens and their associated syndromes to explain the clinical presentation.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) JC polyomavirus - progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy: multifocal non-enhancing white-matter lesions without mass effect, ataxia, hemiparesis, visual and cognitive decline. (2) HIV-1 itself - HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder/HIV encephalopathy: symmetric periventricular white-matter change with atrophy, psychomotor slowing, gait instability. (3) Cytomegalovirus - CMV encephalitis/ventriculoencephalitis (also polyradiculomyelitis): periventricular enhancement, confusion, cranial neuropathies at CD4 <50. (4) Mycobacterium tuberculosis - tuberculous meningitis with basal meningeal enhancement, tuberculomas and infarcts. (Also consider Toxoplasma gondii encephalitis and primary CNS lymphoma, though both typically show ring enhancement and mass effect.)

questions.question: Name two second-line drug options for each of the following.
questions.question_raw: 14. Second Line Drug Options (Name 2 for each): a) PJP Pneumonia; b) CNS Toxoplasma (if can't use pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin); c) Stenotrophomonas pneumonia (if TMP-SMX contraindicated)

parts.text: PJP pneumonia - second-line options.
CNS toxoplasmosis, if pyrimethamine plus sulfadiazine plus leucovorin cannot be used - second-line options.

parts_raw.text: a) PJP Pneumonia - second line options
b) CNS Toxoplasma - second line options

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Clindamycin plus primaquine (preferred alternative; check G6PD). (2) IV pentamidine (severe), or atovaquone / TMP plus dapsone (mild-to-moderate). b) (1) TMP-SMX. (2) Pyrimethamine plus clindamycin plus leucovorin, or atovaquone-based therapy. c) (1) Levofloxacin (or moxifloxacin). (2) Minocycline/tigecycline, or cefiderocol/ceftazidime.
questions.beyond_mandell: CNS toxoplasmosis and Stenotrophomonas alternatives are not in this chapter; they rest on IDSA/CDC OI guidance and standard antimicrobial references.

cohort_answer.text:
Primaquine + Clindamycin (favoured); IV Pentamidine (mild: Dapsone + Trimethoprim)

parts.text: How would you treat PJP, Toxoplasma, and Stenotrophomonas infections if Septra, sulfadiazine, and ticarcillin-clavulanate or Septra respectively were unavailable? Give two treatment options each.
A patient with enterococcal infective endocarditis has high-level aminoglycoside resistance. What is one issue with using streptomycin?

parts_raw.text: How would you treat PJP, Toxoplasma, and Stenotrophomonas infections if Septra, Sulfadiazine, and Ticarcillin/Clav or Septra respectively were not available? (give two treatment options each)
A patient with enterococcus infective endocarditis has high level aminoglycoside resistance. What is one issue with using streptomycin?

questions.model_answer: a) Pneumocystis jirovecii (no TMP-SMX): (1) clindamycin + primaquine; (2) IV pentamidine (severe) or atovaquone (mild-moderate). Toxoplasma (no sulfadiazine): (1) pyrimethamine + clindamycin (with leucovorin); (2) pyrimethamine + atovaquone (or atovaquone monotherapy). Stenotrophomonas maltophilia (no ticarcillin-clavulanate or TMP-SMX): (1) levofloxacin; (2) minocycline (alternatives: cefiderocol, ceftazidime). b) High-level resistance to gentamicin does not predict streptomycin susceptibility, so streptomycin must be tested separately; and if high-level streptomycin resistance is also present, no synergy with a cell-wall-active agent is achievable in vivo (added issues: streptomycin toxicity and limited availability/level monitoring).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the streptomycin/high-level-resistance point is from this chapter; the PJP, Toxoplasma, and Stenotrophomonas regimens rest on standard IDSA/guideline therapy.

cohort_answer.text: PJP (no Septra): Severe: Pentamidine 4mg/kg IV, or Clindamycin 450mg PO q6h + Primaquine 15-30mg PO q24h x21d; Mild-moderate: Atovaquone 750mg PO BID with food x21d. Toxoplasma (no Sulfadiazine): Clindamycin 300mg PO q8h + Pyrimethamine, or Atovaquone 750mg PO BID + pyrimethamine. Stenotrophomonas (no Ticarcillin/Clav or Septra): Minocycline 200mg IV x1 then 100mg IV BID, or Levofloxacin 750mg IV/PO q24h, ceftazidime, colistin, cefiderocol. Streptomycin issue: high level resistance = growth in presence of high concentration of streptomycin or gentamicin, meaning no synergistic AG effect possible in vivo if resistant to both; cannot extrapolate resistance of one aminoglycoside based on the other

questions.question: A woman with HIV (CD4 72) presents with seizure and focal neurologic deficits. CT head shows 3 large gray matter lesions, the largest about 3 cm. You suspect this is due to toxoplasmosis.
questions.question_raw: 18. A woman who has HIV (CD4 72) presents with seizure/focal neurologic deficits. CT head demonstrates 3 large grey matter lesions, largest ~3 cm. You suspect this is due to toxoplasmosis.

parts.text: First-line regimen.
Regimen if 16 weeks pregnant.
Most likely alternative diagnosis.

parts_raw.text: 1st Line Regimen
Regimen if 16 weeks pregnant
Most likely alternative diagnosis

questions.model_answer: a) Pyrimethamine 200 mg PO load, then 50 mg/day (<60 kg) or 75 mg/day (>=60 kg), PLUS sulfadiazine 1000 mg (<60 kg) or 1500 mg (>=60 kg) q6h, PLUS folinic acid 10-20 mg/day (up to 50 mg/day); acute therapy 3-6 weeks then maintenance. b) At 16 weeks (>=14 weeks) the same pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine-folinic acid regimen is acceptable (pyrimethamine avoided only in first trimester); alternative pyrimethamine-clindamycin-folinic acid. c) Primary CNS lymphoma.

cohort_answer.text: 1st line: Pyrimethamine 200mg x1 dose then 75mg/day PO + Sulfadiazine 1.5g PO q6h + Folinic acid 25mg/day; alternative Septra 10mg/kg/day (TMP component) IV/PO divided q12h. If <60kg, Sulfadiazine dose 1g QID. Pregnant (16 weeks): Pyrimethamine 200mg x1 then 75mg/day PO + Sulfadiazine 1.5g PO q6h + Folinic acid 25mg/day; alternative Pyrimethamine + Clindamycin + Leucovorin. Alternative diagnosis: CNS lymphoma; also MTB, Cryptococcus.

questions.question: A man with HIV who has lived in Toronto his entire life is non-adherent to antiretroviral therapy with a CD4 count of 50 cells/uL. He presents with three weeks of altered level of consciousness and ataxia. MRI shows scattered white matter lesions without mass effect.
questions.question_raw: Gentleman with HIV has lived in Toronto his entire life. Noncompliant with ART and CD4 is 50. Presents with 3 weeks of altered LOC and ataxia. MRI shows scattered white matter lesions without mass effect.

parts.text: What are the four most likely organisms and the diseases they cause?

parts_raw.text: What are the 4 most likely organisms and diseases they cause?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) JC polyomavirus - progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (asymmetric, non-enhancing white-matter lesions, no mass effect; diagnosis by CSF JC virus PCR). (2) HIV-1 - HIV encephalopathy/HIV-associated dementia with diffuse symmetric white-matter signal change and atrophy. (3) Cytomegalovirus - CMV encephalitis/ventriculoencephalitis at CD4 <50. (4) Mycobacterium tuberculosis - tuberculous meningoencephalitis with basal meningitis and infarction. Cryptococcus neoformans meningoencephalitis is the other key consideration; Toxoplasma encephalitis and primary CNS lymphoma are less likely given the absence of mass effect.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort lists HSV and VZV as leading answers; in advanced HIV with subacute multifocal white-matter disease and no mass effect, PML, HIV encephalopathy, CMV and tuberculosis are the higher-yield answers.

cohort_answer.text: PML - JC Virus; CMV; HSV; VZV; TB (possible to get hydrocephalus though). Other differentials more likely to have mass effect/increased ICP: Toxoplasmosis, Cryptococcal. Non-infectious ddx: CNS lymphoma (causes mass effect).

questions.model_answer: a) PJP: clindamycin + primaquine; atovaquone (mild) or IV pentamidine (severe). Toxoplasma: pyrimethamine + clindamycin; pyrimethamine + atovaquone (with leucovorin). Stenotrophomonas maltophilia: levofloxacin; minocycline (alternatives cefiderocol, ceftazidime-avibactam plus aztreonam). b) High-level gentamicin resistance does not predict streptomycin susceptibility, so streptomycin must be separately tested; if high-level streptomycin resistance is also present there is no achievable synergy with a cell-wall-active agent (plus streptomycin toxicity/availability and level-monitoring concerns).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the streptomycin point is from this chapter; the PJP, Toxoplasma, and Stenotrophomonas regimens rest on standard IDSA/guideline therapy.

cohort_answer.text: PJP: 1. Clindamycin-primaquine 2. Atovaquone (mild) or TMP-dapsone (mild) 3. IV pentamidine (severe). Toxoplasma: 1. Pyrimethamine-atovaquone 2. Pyrimethamine-clindamycin 3. Septra or atovaquone. Stenotrophomonas: 1. 2 of: Cefiderocol, minocycline, levofloxacin 2. Ceftazidime-avibactam AND aztreonam. b) Need access to lab for rapid streptomycin level testing; need CrCl >50; lack of familiarity amongst clinicians for streptomycin use; drug availability; high rate of ototoxicity which may not be reversible.

questions.question_raw: A 32-year-old woman, who has never left Canada, presents to ED with fevers, confusion, and headache. She is found to have a CD4 count of 72 cells/mm3 and an MRI that shows 2-3 grey matter lesions. A clinical diagnosis of toxoplasmosis is made.

parts.text: What is the first-line treatment for toxoplasmosis?
If this woman were 16 weeks pregnant, what would the first-line treatment be?
What is the MOST likely alternative diagnosis, if not toxoplasmosis?

parts_raw.text: What is the first line treatment for toxoplasmosis?
If this woman was 16 weeks pregnant, what would the first line treatment be?
What is the MOST likely alternative diagnosis, if not toxoplasmosis?

questions.model_answer: a) Pyrimethamine 200 mg PO load, then 50-75 mg/day, PLUS sulfadiazine 1000-1500 mg q6h, PLUS folinic acid 10-20 mg/day (up to 50 mg/day); acute therapy 3-6 weeks then maintenance until CD4 >200 for at least 6 months on ART. b) At 16 weeks (>=14 weeks) the same pyrimethamine-sulfadiazine-folinic acid regimen can be used (pyrimethamine avoided only in the first trimester). c) Primary CNS lymphoma.

questions.question: A 26-year-old man from Nigeria presents with a generalized seizure, no preceding illness or fever, and CT shows a ring-enhancing lesion in the right temporal lobe.
questions.question_raw: Q34. 26M from Nigeria, presents with generalized seizure. No illness or fever preceding. CT shows a ring-enhancing lesion in the R temporal lobe.

parts.text: What are your 2 top diagnoses?

parts_raw.text: A) What are your 2 top diagnoses?

questions.model_answer: (1) Neurocysticercosis — a single enhancing/ring-enhancing parenchymal lesion in a patient from an endemic region, classically presenting with seizure. (2) Cerebral tuberculoma — the other leading cause of a ring-enhancing brain lesion presenting with seizure in an immigrant from a high-TB-burden country. (Consider bacterial abscess, toxoplasmosis if HIV-positive, CNS lymphoma and cryptococcoma in the broader differential.)
questions.beyond_mandell: The competing ring-enhancing-lesion differential (tuberculoma, bacterial abscess, toxoplasmosis, CNS lymphoma, cryptococcoma) is general neuro-ID knowledge; Mandell's chapter addresses only that neurocysticercosis mimics a tumour.

cohort_answer.text: Neurocysticercosis, Tuberculoma, Bacterial abscess, Toxoplasmosis (more in HIV pts; classic CT appearance in 90% of patients is rounded isodense or hypodense lesions with ring enhancement after contrast, multiple in 70-80%, usually at corticomedullary junction and basal ganglia), CNS lymphoma, Cryptococcoma.

questions.question: A 15-year-old with HIV, poorly controlled and off antiretrovirals, presents with focal neurologic signs, seizures, and ring-enhancing lesions. He had Stevens-Johnson syndrome to co-trimoxazole (septra) previously and is not on prophylaxis.
questions.question_raw: 15 year old with HIV, poorly controlled off ARVs. Comes in with focal neurological signs and seizures, ring enhancing lesions. Had SJS to septra previously. Not on ppx.

parts.text: Most likely diagnosis.
Treatment, and when to stop secondary prophylaxis.

parts_raw.text: A) Most likely diagnosis
B) Treatment, when to stop secondary ppx

questions.model_answer: a) CNS toxoplasmosis (toxoplasmic encephalitis). b) Because of the sulfa allergy, use pyrimethamine (200 mg load, then 50-75 mg/day) plus clindamycin (600 mg q6h) plus folinic acid for at least 3-6 weeks, followed by secondary suppression (same agents at reduced dose); add separate PCP prophylaxis (e.g., atovaquone) as clindamycin-pyrimethamine lacks anti-Pneumocystis activity. Stop secondary prophylaxis once CD4 >200 cells/mm3 is sustained for at least 6 months on ART with resolution of signs/symptoms.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort answer says to stop secondary prophylaxis after CD4 >200 for >3 months; Mandell specifies a sustained CD4 >200 for at least 6 months on ART.

cohort_answer.text:
CNS toxoplasmosis
Pyrimethamine + Clindamycin (+leucovorin/folinic acid) x6 weeks then secondary suppression. Stop secondary ppx once CD4 >200 on ARVs for >3 months, no further signs/sx of toxo encephalopathy. Secondary ppx for septra allergy: Atovaquone

parts.text: How would you treat PJP (Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia), Toxoplasma, and Stenotrophomonas if TMP-SMX (Septra), sulfadiazine, and ticarcillin-clavulanic acid/TMP-SMX respectively were not available? Give two options for each.

parts_raw.text: How would you treat PJP, Toxoplasma, and Stenotrophomonas if Septra, Sulfadiazine, and Ticarcillin-clavulanic acid/Septra respectively were not available (2 options each)?

questions.model_answer: a) PJP without TMP-SMX (TMP-SMX is normally first-line): (1) IV pentamidine; (2) clindamycin plus primaquine [atovaquone or trimethoprim-dapsone are further alternatives, typically for mild-to-moderate disease]. b) Toxoplasmosis without sulfadiazine (standard induction is pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin): (1) pyrimethamine + clindamycin + leucovorin (preferred sulfa-sparing regimen); (2) high-dose TMP-SMX (an effective alternative for AIDS-related cerebral toxoplasmosis). c) Stenotrophomonas maltophilia without TMP-SMX or ticarcillin-clavulanate (TMP-SMX is the recommended agent, and TMP-SMX + ticarcillin-clavulanate has been used in cancer patients): (1) levofloxacin (fluoroquinolone); (2) minocycline or tigecycline.
questions.beyond_mandell: The chapter names only TMP-SMX and ticarcillin-clavulanate for S. maltophilia; levofloxacin, minocycline/tigecycline (and cefideromycin) as alternatives rest on IDSA AMR guidance, not this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: PJP (cannot use Septra): Pentamidine; Atovaquone. Toxoplasma (cannot use Sulfadiazine): Pyrimethamine + clindamycin + leucovorin; Atovaquone + septra + leucovorin; Atovaquone +/- pyrimethamine + Septra + leucovorin. Stenotrophomonas (cannot use Ticarcillin-clavulanic acid or Septra): Tigecycline (black box for death); Levofloxacin; Minocycline
